from pypdf import PdfReader
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

        obj=a.get_object()
        action=obj.get('/A')

strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text generation: repeated stimuli across participants and overlapping fMRI windows can undermine claims about generalization to unseen language.

Holding out both subjects and stimuli is a meaningful evaluation target for transfer to new participants and content. The discussion usefully distinguishes EEG sentence samples from overlapping fMRI windows.

The investigation covers two public datasets, Narratives and ZuCo, and two representative models, UniCoRN and EEG2Text. Split diagrams, overlap measurements across four seeds, and implementation details provide a useful starting point for a reproducible evaluation study.
weaknesses: The supplied algorithms do not enforce the central zero-leakage guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks whether a subject belongs to another partition but does not exclude texts assigned to validation/test; its edge-restoration step can therefore reintroduce stimulus overlap. Algorithm 2, line 33, has the complementary omission for subjects. The prose and pseudocode also disagree about graph construction. Correct algorithms and independently verifiable split audits are necessary.

The leakage metrics are inconsistent with their stated interpretation. Equation (8) counts identical Fij elements in the training/test intersection, whereas the paper defines brain-signal leakage as different recordings from a shared subject. Disjoint recordings can therefore have zero intersection despite subject overlap. Its denominator is also zero for genuinely held-out subjects, with no convention specified. These issues prevent reproducing or interpreting Table 1 as written.

Several reported ROUGE scores are mathematically inconsistent with standard F1 aggregation. For example, Table 4 reports EEG2Text precision 23.95, recall 23.98, and F1 25.74; F1 cannot exceed the arithmetic mean of precision and recall, including under ordinary per-example averaging. Multiple Table 3 rows have similar inconsistencies. The scoring implementation and reported results require an audit.

The paper conflates distinct generalization settings with universally invalid evaluation. Subject overlap is inappropriate for claims about unseen participants, but separate recordings from the same participant can support valid within-subject evaluation. Likewise, unseen-subject decoding of familiar stimuli differs from jointly unseen-subject/unseen-stimulus decoding. The blanket claim that all prior splitting methods leak test data should be narrowed to the specific generalization target.

Section 5.2 does not establish the claimed causal damage from leakage. Decreasing validation loss or increasing test BLEU with additional training does not itself demonstrate overfitting. Table 2 changes encoder initialization, learning rate, and training duration together, while different partitions also change evaluation difficulty and potentially training-data volume. Controlled comparisons on a common clean holdout are needed. Claims that encoders contribute little additionally require shuffled-signal or no-signal controls.

The benchmark remains insufficiently reproducible and its utilization claims are unsupported. The manuscript provides no code or split-file link despite claiming a release, no final subject/story allocations or retained/discarded sample counts, and no uncertainty estimates for decoding results. It also does not clearly specify whether evaluation uses free generation or ground-truth prefixes. Extending a fixed partition does not establish globally maximal data retention, and merely changing the evaluation split does not demonstrate improved model generalization. Corrections and targeted reruns are needed before the contribution meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.
